pages.text:
*The Seventh Rule of Mapmaking: A good map has more than one hand in it.*

The shout was only a heron. The clatter, a loose rock tumbling down the scree slope. But the sound had hit the ridge with such force that Master Finch was already moving before her brain caught up with her feet. Her hawthorn cane struck the wet stone, skidded, and vanished into a patch of moss. Then came the stumble. Her foot twisted sharply against the slick ground. A sharp cry, brief and bright, followed by the dull thud of her shoulder hitting the earth.

"Master!" Tam shouted, the word tearing out of her throat before she could think.

She ran, her boots slipping on the damp leaves, but Odd was faster. The ferryman’s son had already dropped his pack and was half-kneeling beside Finch. His red hair was wild in the wind, his face pale, but his hands were steady. He moved with the quick, fluid grace of a boy used to balancing on narrow planks. He slid one arm under her shoulders and the other under her knees.

"Easy, easy," he said, his voice low and urgent. "Don’t fight me. I’ve got you."

Finch made a sound that was half groan, half sigh, and closed her eyes. She did not scream. She did not thrash. She simply went limp, trusting the boy who had only known her for three days to hold her entire weight. Odd lifted her with a grunt of effort, his knees bending, and began the long, slow climb toward the ridge.
pages.image: A tall, thin old woman in a lavender scarf lies on a rocky ridge path, one ankle swollen, while a gangly boy with red hair and a gap-toothed grin carefully lifts her by the shoulders, moss and wind-blown leaves swirling around their feet.

pages.text:
The shepherd’s hut was a low, grey hump of stone that seemed to grow out of the heather. Inside, the air smelled of peat smoke and damp wool. A large, sleepy dog with a patchy brown coat lay curled on a bed of dried grass, watching them with one heavy-lidded eye. It did not bark. It merely yawned, showing a pink tongue that looked like a soft, red leaf.

Finch sat on the edge of the bed, her face the color of old parchment. Her ankle was swollen to the size of a large loaf of bread, the skin tight and shiny over the bone. She looked at it with the detached curiosity of a mapmaker studying a difficult coast.

"I cannot go on," she said. Her voice was gravel in a jar, rough but clear. "The bone is not broken, thank the gods, but it is angry. And I am stubborn."

Tam knelt beside her, her hands hovering, afraid to touch the swelling. "Then what do we do? The survey is in two weeks."

Finch’s eyes snapped to the pigeon cage in the corner. Sixpence ruffled her grey feathers, the white patch on her chest glowing in the dim light.

"Sixpence flies," Finch said. "She carries news. We send her to the Guild. We tell them I am safe, and that the work continues." She leaned forward, her chin resting on her cane. "Tam goes. Odd guides. I stay here, stubborn and comfortable, until the shepherd’s wife comes home with her soup."
pages.image: Inside a dim stone hut, a tall old woman with white hair in a bun sits on a bed of heather, her swollen ankle visible, pointing a hawthorn cane toward a grey pigeon in a wooden cage while a large brown dog watches sleepily.

pages.text:
"No," Tam said.

The word dropped onto the floor like a heavy stone. It was not a shout. It was a refusal that filled the small, smoky room.

"The map belongs to you," Tam said, her voice trembling only slightly. "You built the team. You know the land. I am only the ink-grinder. I grind the ink. I hold the quill while you think. If you cannot walk, we turn back. We go home. It is the sensible thing."

Finch did not answer immediately. She reached for her hawthorn cane, braced it against the uneven stone, and pushed herself upright with a grunt of effort. She swayed, her face the color of old parchment, but she did not fall. She looked at Tam, and for a moment, the old woman seemed taller than the hut.

"You are listening to the wrong voice," Finch said.

"I am listening to my feet," Tam whispered.

"No," Finch said, tapping the cane on the stone. "You are listening to your fear that you began too late. That you are not enough." She took a step, then another, wincing but not stopping. "I did not enter you for my sake, Tam. I entered you for yours. Because I watched you grind that ink for seven months. Because I watched you draw that river, crooked and wobbly, and you kept trying. I believe in your hands. I believe in your eyes. The map is yours. It always was."
pages.image: A sturdy, freckled girl with a black braid tied with blue string stands with her arms crossed, looking down, while a tall old woman in a lavender scarf leans on a hawthorn cane, standing firm in a stone hut doorway, her expression serious and kind.

pages.text:
Finch reached into the deep pocket of her coat. Her fingers, trembling slightly, pulled out a small, round object. It was her spectacles, the ones with the round lenses and the thin gold frames. Tam gasped. Those were Finch’s. She had seen them only when the old woman read the finest charts, the ones with letters so small they looked like a swarm of black ants.

"Keep them," Finch said, pressing them into Tam’s ink-stained palm. "You need to see the small things. The tiny bends. The hidden currents."

Then she took out the brass sextant, heavy and cold, and placed that in Tam’s hand too. But her last offering was different. She reached into her satchel and pulled out a small, oilcloth bundle. It was old. The cloth was faded to the color of weak tea. She opened it carefully, revealing a map. It was drawn on thin parchment, the lines wobbly, the ink faded, the coastline a chaotic squiggle that looked more like a child’s scribble than a survey of the coast.

"This is my first map," Finch said. Her voice was softer now. "I drew it sixty years ago, when I was eleven. I was terrified. I thought I had started too far behind. I thought I would never catch up." She looked at Tam, her eyes bright behind the empty space where her glasses had been. "Carry it. When you feel you are too slow, look at what I drew at eleven, and look at what I draw now. That is the whole of the trade."
pages.image: A small, faded map with wobbly ink lines is held open by an old woman's trembling hands, showing a chaotic coastline drawing, while a young girl with ink-stained fingers reaches out to take the brass sextant and round spectacles beside it.

pages.text:
Tam closed the oilcloth bundle. It felt heavy, heavier than the brass sextant, heavier than the spectacles. It felt like a promise.

"Let’s send Sixpence," Tam said. Her voice was steady.

She took the pigeon from its cage. Sixpence hopped onto her outstretched hand, her grey feathers soft and warm. Tam tied a small scrap of parchment to the bird’s leg. The message was short: *Master Finch is safe. The survey continues. Do not worry.*

Sixpence fluffed her feathers, the white patch on her chest standing out in the dim light. With a flick of her wings, she launched herself from Tam’s hand, spiraling up through the small window of the hut, a grey dart against the grey sky.

Outside, the wind had died. The ridge was quiet. Odd slung his pack over his shoulder, checking the straps. Dumpling, the mule, stood patiently, chewing a mouthful of dried apples, his ears twitching.

Tam picked up her satchel. She held the oilcloth bundle tightly against her chest. She looked back at the hut door, where a small figure in a lavender scarf was waving her cane, a silent, stubborn wave.

It was the first time in Tam’s life that anyone had trusted her with the whole thing.
pages.image: A small grey pigeon with a white chest patch flies out of a stone hut window, while a freckled girl and a red-haired boy watch from the doorway, a grey mule chewing apples nearby, the open moor stretching out in the background.
